answer: Yes. The `export` command defines variables for use in CLI; reference them as ${variable} in any CLI command. Syntax: `export [-h]` and `export [<variable>=[<value>]]`. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. The variable name can be any alphanumeric string; the value can be any supported character, including spaces. Variables are locally defined per session, so they are removed after the session is closed, i.e. they do not survive logout. This is particularly useful in CLI scripts. `export SLOT_NUMBER=2` declares one, `export SLOT_NUMBER=` deletes it, and `export` with no arguments lists all existing variables (for example export MYSESSIONID="10.100.152.29:56154" and export MYUSERNAME="admin").

`shell` launches a Linux bash shell on the node itself, running as the currently logged-in user with that user's command access; certain commands can be run with elevated privileges by prefixing 'sudo' (permitted binaries include /bin/ping, /sbin/reboot, /sbin/shutdown, /bin/netstat, /bin/df, /usr/bin/du, /sbin/dhclient and a set of /opt/infinera/thanos/local/bin scripts). `gshell` launches a bash shell inside a Guest Container instead, with syntax `gshell [-h] [<cmd>]`, and has a pre-condition: the dial-out server must be configured for the command to execute properly. Both are Operational mode, both allow a single command to be passed inline (`shell ifconfig`, `gshell ls -l`), and both return to the CLI prompt on 'exit'.

No. `kill-session <session-id>` closes any established session regardless of type (CLI, NETCONF, etc.), but the <session-id> must match an existing session-id in the form '<ip-address>:<port>' and cannot match the id of the current session. To end your own session use the normal `exit` command instead. Access mode is Operational mode. Use `show session` first to list current sessions and get the id. Example: `kill-session 10.24.11.25:56212`.

Use the `message` command, which sends a message to other CLI sessions: `message [message-content=]<value> [[target=]<value>]`. Access mode is Operational mode. message-content is a string of 1-4096 characters. target defaults to 'all', so a bare `message "System will reboot in 5 minutes"` broadcasts to every CLI session. Other target values are local (only serial console or CRAFT sessions), remote (only remote sessions such as SSH), a specific session-id, or a username (all CLI sessions of that user). Example targeted form: `message "System reboot in 5 minutes" 0.0.0.0:36`. The command can also be executed from NETCONF and RESTCONF, but the message is only ever delivered to CLI sessions.

The `property` commands set or show a type-specific property that the system auto-instantiates but the user can configure. Syntax: `show property-<card-name>/<property-name> [value] [description]` and `set property-<card-name>/<property-name> [value <value>]`, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. Two properties are supported: fast-client-recovery, which indicates whether fast client signal recovery is enabled or disabled in case of client signal failures, with values disabled or enabled and default disabled; and max-packet-length, the maximum packet length supported by the CHM6 / CHM6L DCO, with a range of 1518 to 18000 and default 1518. Example: `set property-1-5/fast-client-recovery value enabled`.

Use `run`, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. Pre-condition: the task or script to be called must already be defined. Syntax: `run task [[task-name=]<value>]` and `run script [-q] [-y] [-e=<value>] [-r] [[script-name=]<value>] [[arguments=]<value>]`. task-name is a leafref to /ioa-ne:ne/ioa-ne:system/ioa-ne:scheduled-tasks/ioa-ne:task/ioa-ne:name; script-name is a relative path within the script directory, with optional arguments. Flags: -q runs the script quietly (only command output, not the commands themselves), -r executes the script as a declarative config script that replaces system configuration with the script content, and -e sets the error option: continue (default), stop, or rollback. Examples: `run task collect-diag`, `run script config.cli -e=stop -q`.

Both add, set, show and delete user-configurable scheduled commands in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode, and both use the same core attributes: enabled (true/false, default true), command (string), command-type (CLI command), frequency in w/d/h/m/s, start-time, end-time, persistent (true/false, default true) plus read-back task-status, next-run, previous-run, previous-result and previous-output. `task` is the richer form: `add task-<name> command <value> ...` also takes label, alarm-report-control (allowed/inhibited, default allowed) and number-of-runs (1..65535 or no-limit), and reports task-status as scheduled, disabled, finished or ongoing with previous-result success/fail. `scheduled-task` is addressed as scheduled-task-<name>, listed with `show scheduled-tasks`, and an empty frequency means a single-occurrence task.

Only if you are an SA user. `show session` lists currently established management layer sessions; only SA users can access the list of all sessions, and remaining users can only see their own session. Syntax: `show session-<session-id> [session-user] [session-type] [session-protocol] [created-time] [local-ip-address] [dial-out-server-name]`, available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. session-id is the IP address and transport port of the session, or 'NA' if initiated from the serial port. session-type can be cli, snmp, netconf, restconf, webgui or gnmi; session-protocol can be telnet, telnet-raw, serial, ssh, ssh-raw, https or http. RESTCONF sessions appear in CLI when Cookie Based Authentication is used; the default keep-alive is 5 minutes, changeable with the restconf cookie-timeout attribute.

Yes. `set [-f|-v] [<entity id>] <attribute> <value> [<attribute> <value> ...] [<filter> ...]` accepts wildcards (*) to set an attribute on multiple instances at once: as replacement of the whole instance key (card-*), of a single instance key (port-1-4-*, port-1-*-3), of all following keys to the right (odu-1-4,5,6,7-*), for auto-completing instance keys (user-admin*, ethernet-*), and for auto-completing attribute names (admin* for admin-state). Ranges use [] (card-1-[1..4]) and lists too (interface-[DCN,CRAFT]). Filters in the form <attribute>=<value> restrict the set to matching entities, e.g. `set port port-type=line admin-state lock`. All pairs must belong to the same managed entity; if no entity id is given the currently scoped entity is used. The command asks for confirmation when the request may have traffic impact or implicitly affects multiple instances; -f forces without confirmation and -v only validates.

User access to the `shell` command can be limited to users in the NA, NE and TT user-groups. The command launches a Linux bash shell from within the CLI in Operational mode, syntax `shell [-h] [shell command]`. The shell is launched as the currently logged-in user and allows only the commands accessible to that user; exiting the shell (for example with 'exit') returns to the CLI prompt. Certain commands can be run with elevated privileges by prefixing 'sudo', limited to a fixed list including /bin/ping, /sbin/reboot, /sbin/shutdown, /bin/netstat, /bin/df, /usr/bin/du, /sbin/dhclient and scripts under /opt/infinera/thanos/local/bin such as download.sh, config_ip.sh and docker.sh. A single command can be passed inline, e.g. `shell 'sudo netstat -alnp | grep sshd'`.

Yes. If a user executes a `show` command that generates more than 50000 objects, an error message is displayed to indicate that the output is too large. Narrow the request instead: give a specific <entity-id> rather than an <entity-type>, use filters (<attribute>=<value>), name individual attributes, or limit recursion with -r=<n> (full recursion if n is omitted). Other flags that reduce output are -c (container instances only), -a (attributes only), -x (configuration/read-write attributes only) and -o (state/read-only attributes only); -l gives long display, -t tabular format and -d shows default values. Piping to `| more` pages long output. Since R9.0 show output is sorted numerically.

Yes, with `simulate`, in Operational mode: `simulate [trigger=]<value> ([holder-AID=]<value> [type=]<value> [[subtype=]<value>] | [alarmed-entity=]<value> [alarm-type=]<value> [[alarm-direction=]<value>] [[alarm-location=]<value>])`. Triggers are raise-alarm, clear-alarm, plug-in-fru and plug-out-fru; note that plug-out-fru is not supported. Equipment simulation needs the holder-AID matching the card slot or TOM port (string 1..64) and, for plug-in, the card type, with subtype optional. For alarms, alarmed-entity and alarm-type are given; if either is omitted when clearing, all simulated alarms are cleared. alarm-direction and alarm-location default to auto, selected automatically by the system. The command works in a simulator and on a real system, but simulation cannot interfere with real hardware, for example you cannot simulate plug-out of hardware physically present. Example: `simulate plug-in-fru 1-5`.

Yes. The `sleep` command specifies a delay for a specified amount of time, and the sleep time may be an arbitrary floating point number. Syntax: `sleep <time in seconds>` (plus `sleep -h` for help). Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. The single parameter is the duration of delay in seconds. `sleep 1` waits one second and `sleep 0.1` waits 100 milliseconds.

Add a task with no frequency: leaving frequency unset makes it a single-occurrence task that runs once at start-time. Syntax: `add task-<name> command <value> [enabled <value>] [label <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>] [command-type <value>] [frequency <value>] [number-of-runs <value>] [start-time <value>] [end-time <value>] [persistent <value>]`. name is up to 64 characters, command is 1..1024 characters, command-type defaults to cli, enabled defaults to true, persistent defaults to true so the task survives a system restart, alarm-report-control defaults to allowed, and end-time defaults to never. Documented example: `add task-db_backup_once command "upload database file-server=xfr1" start-time 2021-04-23T05:05:00+00:00 alarm-report-control allowed label "DB Backup once"`. The file server xfr1 must be configured before this command is used. task-status shows finished once a single-occurrence task has executed.

`terminate` stops a running operation, in Operational mode. Forms: `terminate location-led <entity>` (a chassis or a card; no effect if no location led test is active there), `terminate otdr [entity=]<value>` for an ongoing OTDR measurement on a port, `terminate otdr-fiber-check [entity=]<value>` for a manually triggered OTDR-based Raman fiber check on an OTS-R entity, `terminate loopback [entity=]<value>[,<value>]*` for WSS loopback on NMC entities (all channels under the loopback in a degree must be terminated, and channels cannot be added or removed while a loopback is active), and `terminate cable-id` for a CableID verification test. Aborting OTDR restores otdr ne function attributes and reverts ots-r-auto-otdr auto-otdr-state, re-raising PUMPS-DISABLED-OTDR-TEST-FAILED if it was fail. CableID verification stops only after the current port-pair completes (maximum delay one port-pair verification time); confirm with `show cable-id cable-id-status` that cable-id-state is idle.

`update` does not assign an arbitrary value the way `set` does; it triggers a predefined update action on an object attribute according to the provided <type>. Syntax: `update [type=]<value> [[entity-id=]<value>[,<value>]*]`, Operational mode only, and multiple instances can be selected with a wildcard (*). The four types are span-loss-alarm-threshold (re-evaluates the OTS attribute span-loss-alarm-threshold), filter-insertion-date-now (updates the chassis dust filter insertion date to the current date), set-under-commissioning (sets the entity to under commissioning state, applicable to NE entities in SLTE systems) and clear-under-commissioning (sets the entity to Ready for Service state, likewise for SLTE NEs). Examples: `update span-loss-alarm-threshold ots-1-1-dwdm-line` and `update filter-insertion-date-now chassis`.

Use the auxiliary commands `tic` and `toc`. `tic` starts a timer for the typed command and `toc` displays the elapsed time since the timer was started and the command was executed by the system. Both are available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. For a single command, chain them on one line separated by semicolons: `tic;show log;toc`. The same pattern works for a list of commands in a script, for example `tic ;show log ;traceroute 10.128.1.1 ;toc`, which times the whole sequence.

Yes. Use `help -s <keyword> [<keyword> ...]`, which searches the provided keyword(s) in all commands' help text and displays the matches in order of relevance. Partial keywords can be given with a wild card, for example `help -s inventory` or `help -s data*`. Related help forms: `help <command/container/attribute>` shows how that item can be used (`help show`); '?' on its own lists all available commands; `<command> ?` lists the addressable parameters for a command (`show ?`); `<command> -?` lists its options (`show -?`); `<command> -h` gives the complete help (`show -h`); `<command> <container> ?` shows the sub-containers and attribute list of a container; and `<command> <attribute> ?` lists the attributes of a container.

Yes to both: aliases are persistent and shared among all users and CLI sessions. The `alias` command defines a friendlier alphanumeric string for one or more commands, containers, attributes or values, in Operational mode. Syntax: `alias [-h]` and `alias [<name>=<value>]`. With no arguments it prints the current list of aliases in the form 'name=value'. Multi-word values must be quoted, and aliases can reference other aliases; an alias <name> can be used without resolving it by quoting it. Examples: `alias s=show` and `alias sa='show alarm'`. Remove aliases with `unalias`.

Run `unalias -a`, which removes all defined aliases. The `unalias` command removes previously defined aliases in Operational mode; syntax is `unalias -h`, `unalias -a`, or `unalias [<name> ...]`, so you can also drop specific ones, e.g. `unalias foo` or `unalias bar baz qux`. Removing an alias has impact on all sessions and users, because aliases are persistent and shared among all users and CLI sessions. The command is always successful unless a supplied <name> is not a defined alias. Use `alias` with no arguments to list what is currently defined before clearing.

`tree` displays the managed entity hierarchy in a depth-indented tree-like format, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. Syntax: `tree [-h]` and `tree [-a|-o|-d=depth] ([<entity id> ...])`. Use -d=depth to cap the maximum display depth, i.e. the number of levels shown; if it is not specified all levels are displayed by default, for example `tree -d=2`. Use -a to display the target entity along with all its ancestors only, for example `tree -a interface-DCN` or `tree -a port usb`. -o displays the YANG tree of the provided top node. The base of the tree is the current working entity or the provided entity id, only managed entities and their instances are shown (no attribute names or values), and output uses the UTF-8 character set. Page long output with `tree | more`.

`edit <entity-id> [<entity-id> ...]` navigates to any entity in the managed entity hierarchy; the entity IDs can be absolute (from the system root) or relative to the current entity in the path banner, and editing a nonexistent instance fails. Examples: `edit card-1-1`, `edit port-1-5-T1`, or relative `edit chassis-1 slot-2`. `up` moves the current path up exactly one level, to the parent of the currently selected entity, and takes no parameters. `top` jumps straight back to the top of the hierarchy, the [ne] root. All three are available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode, take only the -h flag, and their effect is visible on the CLI path banner, e.g. [ chassis-1 ] after `edit chassis-1` and [ ne ] after `top`.

Run `history`, which displays the current session's command history as a numbered list, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode (the only flag is -h). Repeat any entry with '!<n>', where n is the number in the history list, and repeat the immediately previous command with '!!'. To find a particular entry in a long history, filter it with a piped command, for example `history | include 'show'`.

Nothing happens. At the hierarchy top level the `up` command has no impact. `up` brings the current path up by one path level, changing the currently selected managed entity to its parent, and its effect is visible on the CLI banner; once the banner shows the root [ ne ] there is no parent to move to. The command supports no parameters other than -h and is available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Related commands are `edit`, which navigates to any entity in the hierarchy, and `top`, which returns directly to the hierarchy root.

Functionally they are the same command: both `| grep <filter>` and `| include <filter>` display only lines matching the filter, the guide states each is the same as the other, both accept multi-word filters when quoted, both support regex, both do a case-insensitive comparison (`show | grep abc` equals `show | grep ABC`), and both can be chained with other piped commands. The difference is that grep has several additional filtering options: -a=<n> shows n lines of context after each match, -b=<n> shows n lines of context before each match, and -n displays line numbers in the result. So the syntax is `<command> | grep [<option>] <filter>` versus `<command> | include <filter>`. Related filters are exclude (drops matching lines), begin and until.
